words: لَهَا مَا كَسَبَتْ وَعَلَيْهَا مَا ٱكْتَسَبَتْ
rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: The Muʿtazilites infer that people create their own acts: attributing good and evil to them would be invalid if God created those acts, as with involuntary traits.
rows.anchor: المعتزلة احتجوا بهذه الآية على أن فعل العبد بإيجاده وتكوينه

rows.speaker: القاضي
rows.claim: The Qadi argues that if God creates human acts, obligation loses its purpose; on that view, asking for lighter duties is also pointless because God creates both burdens and ease without fatigue.
rows.anchor: لو كان خالقا أفعالهم فما الفائدة في التكليف

words: لَهَا مَا كَسَبَتْ وَعَلَيْهَا مَا ٱكْتَسَبَتْ
rows.speaker: أصحابنا
rows.claim: The author’s school rejects moral annihilation: reward for good and liability for evil can coexist, and the arrival of one does not erase the other.
rows.anchor: احتج أصحابنا بهذه الآية على فساد القول بالمحابطة

words: لَهَا مَا كَسَبَتْ وَعَلَيْهَا مَا ٱكْتَسَبَتْ
rows.speaker: الجبائي
rows.claim: Al-Jubbaʾi reads the verse conditionally: reward remains only if not invalidated, and punishment only if not expiated by repentance, since pure everlasting reward and punishment cannot coexist.
rows.anchor: ظاهر الآية وإن دل على الإطلاق إلا أنه مشروط والتقدير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Razi says the debate over annulment was treated fully under the prohibition on nullifying charity through reproach and injury.
rows.anchor: أن الكلام على هذه المسألة مر على الاستقصاء في تفسير

words: لَهَا مَا كَسَبَتْ وَعَلَيْهَا مَا ٱكْتَسَبَتْ
rows.speaker: كثير من المتكلمين
rows.claim: Many theologians use the verse to argue that God does not punish children for their parents’ sins, as also stated by 6:164.
rows.anchor: احتج كثير من المتكلمين بهذه الآية على أن الله تعالى لا يعذب الأطفال بذنوب آبائهم

rows.speaker: الفقهاء
rows.claim: Jurists infer that ownership ordinarily continues and remains attached to what a person has acquired.
rows.anchor: الفقهاء تمسكوا بهذه الآية في إثبات أن الأصل في الإمساك البقاء والاستمرار

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A Prophetic report says each person has a stronger claim to their earnings than their parents, children, or other people; al-Razi gives no grading.
rows.anchor: وتأكد ذلك بقوله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A guarantor’s payment does not transfer ownership of the guaranteed property: the original basis for ownership remains, while usurpation or liability does not remove it, as illustrated by an umm walad and a mudabbara.
rows.anchor: أن المضمونات لا تملك بأداء الضمان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Incorporating a usurped yard into a building or milling usurped grain does not extinguish the owner’s title.
rows.anchor: إذا غصب ساحة وأدرجها في بنائه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A neighbor has no right of preemption: a co-owner has priority, the parties are not equal, neighborly harm is less, and a neighbor’s sale requires no partition.
rows.anchor: ومنها أنه لا شفعة للجار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Amputation does not end ownership or the duty to compensate; if stolen property still exists, it must be returned to its owner.
rows.anchor: ومنها أن القطع لا يمنع وجوب الضمان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those denying obligatory zakat cite the verse, but al-Razi answers that the specific proofs requiring zakat take precedence over this general text.
rows.anchor: ومنها أن منكري وجوب الزكاة احتجوا به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Razi calls this verse a major foundation for numerous branches of jurisprudence.
rows.anchor: فهذه الآية أصل كبير في فروع الفقه

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A Prophetic report calls supplication the core of worship; al-Razi states no grading.
rows.anchor: لأنه صلى الله عليه وسلم قال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Supplication displays the worshipper’s poverty, need, and humility before God’s majesty and self-sufficiency, so the surah closes with entreaty; al-Razi discusses prayer under 2:186.
rows.anchor: ختم هذه السورة الشريفة المشتملة على هذه العلوم العظيمة بالدعاء والتضرع إلى الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Razi counts four kinds of supplication: the first three begin with “Our Lord,” while the fourth omits that vocative.
rows.anchor: أنه تعالى حكى عن المؤمنين دعاءهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Do not take us to account” means “do not punish us.”
rows.anchor: لا تؤاخذنا أي لا تعاقبنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation for the reciprocal form is that the forgetful person exposed himself to harm through his own action, making the punisher seem to assist in harming him.
rows.anchor: لأن الناسي قد أمكن من نفسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Razi’s alternative is that God takes the sinner through punishment while the sinner clings to God for pardon, so each is figuratively taking the other.
rows.anchor: وعندي فيه وجه آخر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first of two interpretations takes forgetfulness in its ordinary sense, as the opposite of remembering.
rows.anchor: في النسيان وجهان الأول : أن المراد منه

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A Prophetic report says error, forgetfulness, and coercion have been lifted from the community; al-Razi gives no grading.
rows.anchor: رفع عن أمتي الخطأ والنسيان وما استكرهوا عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Razi answers that forgetfulness may be culpable when someone neglects precautions, but excusable when warning signs were absent or the person took reasonable care; he gives examples involving impurity, mistaken shooting, and forgetting memorized Qurʾan.
rows.anchor: ثبت أن النسيان على قسمين

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report says the Prophet tied a thread around his finger when he wanted to remember a need; al-Razi uses it to show deliberate memory precautions.
rows.anchor: وروي أنه صلى الله عليه وسلم كان إذا أراد أن يذكر حاجته شد خيطا في أصبعه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prayer may be hypothetical: these righteous believers only risked such lapses inadvertently, so they disclaim liability even if inadvertent acts could in principle be punished.
rows.anchor: أن يكون هذا دعاء على سبيل التقدير وذلك لأن هؤلاء المؤمنين الذين ذكروا هذا الدعاء كانوا متقين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Supplication can express humility rather than ask for an uncertain outcome; al-Razi compares requests for just judgment, fulfillment of promises, and forgiveness for repentant believers.
rows.anchor: المقصود من الدعاء إظهار التضرع إلى الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Punishing a forgetful person is not rationally impossible: fear of later punishment can sustain memory, though constant vigilance is difficult, making a request for pardon fitting.
rows.anchor: أن مؤاخذة الناسي غير ممتنعة عقلا

rows.speaker: أصحابنا
rows.claim: Al-Razi’s Ashʿari associates argue that the verse supports the rational possibility of obligating what cannot be done: a forgetful person cannot avoid the act, yet asks God not to punish him for it.
rows.anchor: أصحابنا الذين يجوزون تكليف ما لا يطاق يتمسكون بهذه الآية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second sense of forgetfulness is abandonment, supported by Qurʾanic usage at 20:115 and 9:67.
rows.anchor: والقول الثاني : في تفسير النسيان ، أن يحمل على الترك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the abandonment reading, error means doing an act on the basis of a mistaken interpretation.
rows.anchor: والمراد بالخطأ ، أن يفعل الفعل لتأويل فاسد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If forgetting and error mean intentionally doing wrong, the commanded prayer gives grave sinners grounds to hope for pardon: God instructs believers to ask not to be punished for such sins.
rows.anchor: فأما الاحتمال الأول فإنه يدل على حصول العفو لأصحاب الكبائر

rows.speaker: الخصم
rows.claim: The alternative cases, where one or both terms mean an unintentional act, are excluded within the opponent’s premises, since punishment would be wrong and cannot properly be requested.
rows.anchor: وأما القسم الثاني والثالث فباطلان لأن المؤاخذة على ذلك قبيحة عند الخصم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although neglecting precautions may be culpable, the person is then punished for deliberately failing to take care, not for the lapse itself; the verse therefore still supports hope of pardon for grave sinners.
rows.anchor: فهو في الحقيقة مؤاخذ بترك التحفظ قصدا وعمدا

rows.speaker: النابغة
rows.claim: Al-Nabigha’s verse uses isr for a burden borne to shield a tribe from oppression, evidencing the word’s sense of weight and hardship.
rows.anchor: قال النابغة : يا مانع الضيم أن يغشى سراتهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A covenant is called an isr because it is weighty; 3:81 uses the word for God’s covenant and pact.
rows.anchor: ثم سمي العهد إصرا لأنه ثقيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Isr can also mean affection or kinship: caring for someone makes the hardships that befall them weigh on one’s heart.
rows.anchor: والإصر العطف ، يقال : ما يأصرني عليه آصرة

rows.speaker: أهل التفسير
rows.claim: Exegetes explain the prayer as asking not to impose the severe obligations placed on Jews: traditions cited include fifty prayers, a quarter of wealth in alms, cutting away garment impurity, worldly penalties for lapses, and loss of formerly lawful foods.
rows.anchor: أهل التفسير فيه وجهين الأول : لا تشدد علينا في التكاليف

rows.speaker: القفال
rows.claim: Al-Qaffal says examining the fifth book of the Torah claimed by the Jews reveals many severe covenants and remarkable details.
rows.anchor: ومن نظر في السفر الخامس من التوراة التي تدعيها هؤلاء اليهود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Razi says God removed such burdens and shackles from this community, citing the description at 7:157.
rows.anchor: ويضع عنهم إصرهم والأغلال التى كانت عليهم

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A Prophetic report says the community was spared transformation, landslides, and drowning; al-Razi gives no grading.
rows.anchor: رفع عن أمتي المسخ والخسف والغرق

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A Prophetic report describes his mission as the tolerant, easy monotheistic way; al-Razi gives no grading.
rows.anchor: وقال عليه الصلاة والسلام : ( بعثت بالحنيفية السهلة السمحة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Believers request easier obligations because severity invites shortcoming, which brings punishment they cannot endure; hence they ask for ease in duties.
rows.anchor: التشديد مظنة التقصير ، والتقصير موجب للعقوبة

rows.speaker: أهل التفسير
rows.claim: The second interpretation asks that God not impose a covenant as severe as that imposed on earlier people; al-Razi says it essentially returns to the first view with an extra unstated element, so the first is preferable.
rows.anchor: والقول الثاني : لا تحمل علينا عهدا وميثاقا يشبه ميثاق من قبلنا

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: The Muʿtazilites say different duties suit different people: Jews’ harsh temperaments required severe commands, whereas this community’s refined character made lighter duties beneficial.
rows.anchor: قالت المعتزلة : من الجائز أن يكون الشيء مصلحة في حق إنسان

rows.speaker: أصحابنا
rows.claim: Al-Razi’s associates answer by asking why God gave Jews harsh natures and this community refined ones; the explanation merely shifts the question about divine choice.
rows.anchor: أجاب الأصحاب بأن السؤال الذي ذكرناه في المقام الأول ننقله إلى المقام الثاني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Razi rejects the Muʿtazilite temperamental explanation as unsound, affirming that God acts as He wills and is not questioned, as stated at 21:23.
rows.anchor: ومن تأمل وأنصف علم أن هذه التعليلات عليلة فجل جناب الجلال عن أن يوزن بميزان الاعتزال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭāqa is a verbal noun from iṭāqa, like ṭāʿa from iṭāʿa and ijāba from ijāba, and is used in place of the verbal noun.
rows.anchor: الطاقة اسم من الإطاقة ، كالطاعة من الإطاعة

rows.speaker: أصحابنا
rows.claim: Al-Razi’s associates argue that the prayer proves the rational permissibility of imposing an obligation beyond capacity, since it asks God to refrain from it.
rows.anchor: من الأصحاب من تمسك به في أن تكليف ما لا يطاق جائز إذ لو لم يكن جائزا لما حسن طلبه بالدعاء

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: The Muʿtazilites read “beyond our capacity” as an act that is extremely difficult, as in colloquial claims of being unable to look at someone or bear a task.
rows.anchor: ما لا طاقة لنا به } أي يشق فعله مشقة عظيمة

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: The cited poem uses ṭāqa for what is difficult to bear, supporting the Muʿtazilite reading of the phrase as severe hardship.
rows.anchor: قال الشاعر : إنك إن كلفتني ما لم أطق

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A Prophetic report says a servant should receive food and clothing and not be assigned work beyond what he can bear; al-Razi cites it for the hardship sense and gives no grading.
rows.anchor: أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قال في المملوك

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Imran ibn Husayn reports that the Prophet instructed the ill to pray sitting, or on their side if unable; jurists read inability as severe hardship, not literal incapacity. No grading is stated.
rows.anchor: أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قال

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: The Muʿtazilites read “they could not hear” at 11:20 as meaning that hearing was difficult for them.
rows.anchor: أجاب المعتزلة عنه من وجوه الأول

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: Their second reply says taḥmīl is placing an unbearable load, so the phrase means punishment that cannot be endured; reading it as obligation is figurative.
rows.anchor: التحميل هو أن يضع عليه ما لا طاقة له بتحمله فيكون المراد منه العذاب

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: Their third reply is that praying against an act does not establish that God could do it, just as prayers against unjust judgment, disgrace, disobedience, or loss of deeds do not establish those outcomes as possible.
rows.anchor: هب أنهم سألوا الله تعالى أن لا يكلفهم بما لا قدرة لهم عليه لكن ذلك لا يدل على جواز أن يفعل خلافه

rows.speaker: أصحابنا
rows.claim: Al-Razi’s school rejects the hardship-only gloss: it would duplicate the preceding prayer, and ṭāqa means ability, so the apparent sense is what one has no power to do; “hard” is only figurative.
rows.anchor: محمولا على أن لا يشدد عليهم في التكليف

rows.speaker: أصحابنا
rows.claim: They answer that Qurʾanic usage associates bearing with obligation, as in the human bearing of the trust at 33:72; even without that idiom, the phrase covers both punishment and obligation, so narrowing it needs proof.
rows.anchor: التحمل مخصوص في عرف القرآن بالتكليف

rows.speaker: أصحابنا
rows.claim: They argue that a genuinely impossible act cannot be requested in supplication, like combining opposites or making the eternal originated; abandoning this rule in particular cases needs specific evidence.
rows.anchor: فعل الشيء إذا كان ممتنعا لم يجز طلب الامتناع منه على سبيل الدعاء والتضرع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A difficult burden can be carried or imposed, while what is beyond capacity cannot be carried at all; therefore the verse uses “impose” for the impossible and both verbs for hardship.
rows.anchor: الشاق يمكن حمله أما ما لا يكون مقدورا

words: لَا تُحَمِّلْنَا مَا لَا طَاقَةَ لَنَا بِهِۦ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Razi imagines two stations: outward religious law asks for no severe duties; the beginning of unveiling asks not to demand praise, gratitude, or knowledge commensurate with divine majesty, which humans cannot attain. Law precedes inner reality, explaining the order.
rows.anchor: للعبد مقامين أحدهما : قيامه بظاهر الشريعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plural prayer seeks fuller acceptance: when people’s spiritual intentions and desires converge on one request, its realization is stronger.
rows.anchor: المقصود منه ببيان أن قبول الدعاء عند الاجتماع أكمل وذلك لأن للهمم تأثيرات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fourth prayer omits “Our Lord” because a call is needed at a distance; its omission signals that persistent entreaty brings the servant near to God.
rows.anchor: إنما يحتاج إليه عند البعد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAfw means removing punishment, whereas maghfira conceals the sin and protects the sinner from the shame and exposure of punishment in the grave.
rows.anchor: العفو أن يسقط عنه العقاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After seeking release from bodily punishment and spiritual disgrace, believers seek reward: mercy asks for bodily delights of Paradise, while “You are our Protector” asks for spiritual reward culminating in witnessing divine majesty.
rows.anchor: فلما تخلص منهما أقبل على طلب الثواب

rows.speaker: كثير من المتكلمين
rows.claim: Some theologians reduce these requests to acts of obedience; al-Razi grants this as the limit of their knowledge while retaining the deeper bodily and spiritual interpretation.
rows.anchor: كثيرا من المتكلمين يستبعدون هذه الكلمات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling God their Mawla expresses utmost humility and dependence: God gives every blessing and honor, as a guardian tends a child or a master orders a servant’s affairs.
rows.anchor: هذه الكلمة تدل على نهاية الخضوع والتذلل والاعتراف بأنه سبحانه هو المتولي لكل نعمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here Mawla means helper or protector, as in 8:40, 2:257, 66:4, and 47:11.
rows.anchor: وقوله { فإن الله هو مولاه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The requested victory includes military struggle, debate by proof, and Islam’s political ascendancy over other religions, as promised at 9:33.
rows.anchor: انصرنا عليهم في محاربتنا معهم

rows.speaker: المحققون
rows.claim: Some spiritual authorities interpret victory as God’s angelic, spiritual power overcoming bodily forces that urge the soul toward what is other than God.
rows.anchor: ومن المحققين من قال : { فانصرنا على القوم الكافرين } المراد منه إعانة الله بالقوة الروحانية الملكية

rows.speaker: مقاتل بن سليمان
rows.claim: Al-Wahidi transmits from Muqatil a report that during the night journey the Prophet received the closing verses of al-Baqara and Gabriel taught him these prayers; God answered each petition with forgiveness, no burden, and victory. Some versions add that angels said “Amen”; no grading is given.
rows.anchor: وروى الواحدي رحمه الله عن مقاتل بن سليمان أنه لما أسري بالنبي صلى الله عليه وسلم إلى السماء أعطى خواتيم سورة البقرة
